doc.title: Dave Liebman — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Declining Joe Farrell's Plaza Hotel gig and studio work
summary: Farrell offered him a Plaza double; Liebman declined, closing the door on studio work, and worried about making a living on Elvin's pay.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: I’ve heard Kenny Berger – Kenny Berger told me that Joe is a cold fish.

It appeared that way, but maybe it was personal. He didn’t like me. I don’t know. The only time I got anything out of Joe was – and it was heavy, because it kind of determined the course of my life. In this period, he called. Again, the phone. “It’s Joe Farrell,” Elena, “Joe.” He goes, “I got a double at the Plaza, Sunday night.” Something like that. No hello, no nothing. “Double,” meaning, “I got something else. Do you want to take my place?” The Plaza Hotel. You know what that means. That’s top. That’s tuxedo. That’s going to be with the Lew Soloffs of the world and the Snooky Youngs. That is the studio clique, because that Plaza Hotel, it’s going to be the top gig. And I know. I could – I knew right there, because the studio thing was very big then. I knew that this was – this is a yes or no, and this would determine the – I could feel that. I said, “Could I have a second?” He said, “Come on. Hurry up.” I said, “Elena, this is a chance.” If I do good, which I figured I would, I could walk into the studio situation, which Joe was in, and I could be that thing, which was a very big thing in the ’60s and ’70s. If I say no, that’s it, because once you say no, you’re off the list, and they don’t forget. She said, “What do you . . . ?” I said, “I don’t want – the studio thing’s the last thing I want to do.” She said, “Then tell them no.” So I said okay. “Okay, Joe, I can’t make it.” Bump. You just closed the door, boy. Don’t you ever come around this place anymore. That was the end of my studio, any desire or chance I might have had to go into studio work. That was the closest I ever got to Joe Farrell.
The irony is, considering what happened to studio work in New York in the ’70s, and you know what happened with Joe.
Yeah, not the worst thing. But at that time . . .
Because guys were making some bread.

And Elvin was 300 a week or something. We weren’t making any money. I was – I’m starting to think about how am I going to live? This question’s starting to dawn on me, that I’m not a kid anymore. How do I make a living?
Also, by the way, at that same place I later heard Novella Nelson, who was – she wasn’t a jazz person, but she was a good singer-actress.
I’m glad you told me that. That completes the cycle from that Thanksgiving night with Pete.
